text: The cyclo is rented, not owned, and that arrangement governs every hour of the boy's day. He pedals his bicycle taxi through Ho Chi Minh City in the mid-nineties, paying out to the Madame who holds the machine, feeding two sisters and a grandfather on whatever is left over. Trần Anh Hùng shot it in Vietnamese with French financing, and the city arrives as heat and noise rather than as explanation. What the 123 minutes make room for is arithmetic: how many fares, how many hours, how thin the margin between the rent on a vehicle and the work somebody else is willing to offer instead. Crime is a job here, not a temptation, and it comes with an employer. The Golden Lion went to it in 1995, though the film stays occupied with what a day of pedalling actually buys.

Rome, 1945: a journalist who cannot quite cover his rent spends the film going back over an arrangement made when he was a child. He was raised by a poor, warm-hearted grandmother; his younger brother was taken into an aristocrat's house and brought up as a gentleman. Italy could split one family that cleanly, and Valerio Zurlini treats the split as an injury that never closes over. Thrown together again in the Florence of the 1930s, the elder appoints himself keeper of a brother he resents, and obligation does the work that affection cannot. Hatred and love are not alternating moods in Cronaca familiare. They are one feeling, held at the same time, for years. A hundred and eight minutes, nearly all of it recollection, and a Golden Lion to its name.

Pietro has come north from Sicily to train as a teacher; Giovanni, who cannot read, has come to pay for it. Gianni Amelio spends 124 minutes watching that arrangement hold and then chafe. Italy in the 1950s is moving its southerners toward its northern cities, and this family reorganises around the one member who might emerge with a certificate: the illiterate brother taking whatever work is hardest, the educated one accumulating a debt nobody itemises. Gratitude gets heavy. Amelio is exact about the direction the sacrifice runs and unsentimental about what it does to the man making it, until love inside the household becomes hard to separate from investment in it. What stands to be lost is not the certificate but the brother who bought it. The Golden Lion went to the film in 1998.

A jury prize for direction and an audience award: a split verdict of the friendlier kind, and an odd one for a picture in which a blind masseur takes on a town's two gangs. Takeshi Kitano keeps three trades in play at once, massage and dice and the sword, and declines to let the third automatically outrank the other two. The village is what the gangs are fighting over, the townspeople are the ones paying for it, and the 116 minutes move at the speed of a man with nowhere in particular to be. Violence, when it arrives, is fast and out of proportion to whatever preceded it. What holds the film together is timing, the pause before a strike rather than the strike, and a period setting treated as a place where people are trying to get through the week.

She sings at night in Kinshasa bars, and a room pays what a room pays. Then her fourteen-year-old is hurt, money has to come from somewhere, and the film becomes a search conducted on foot across a city that never lowers its volume. Alain Gomis works in Lingala over 123 minutes, sliding out of the errand and into music again and again: the band, the rehearsal, a stretch of dreaming that arrives without warning and refuses to account for itself. The tension is not whether the sum gets found. It is what a proud woman will bring herself to ask for, and from whom, and what the asking costs her afterwards. Félicité holds a Silver Bear Grand Jury Prize and the Étalon d'Or de Yennenga. The accident is the plot; the singing is the film.

The route from West Africa to Italy is less a distance than a sequence of men who have to be paid. Matteo Garrone films it as an adventure, checkpoints and the Sahara and then open water, and the genre is not decoration: adventure presumes a protagonist with decisions to make, and the two Senegalese teenagers go on making them well past the point where the choices are between good options. They are not fleeing a catastrophe the film bothers to itemise. They want more than what is on offer, which is the motive most accounts of this crossing decline to grant. Garrone took a Silver Lion for the direction and the David di Donatello for best film. The 121 minutes belong to the boys and to the running cost of each stage of the passage.

A puppet stage is a small business, and it went on taking bookings through the Japanese occupation of Taiwan. Hou Hsiao-hsien gives 143 minutes to one puppeteer's working life across the first half of the century, apprenticeship and troupes and audiences and the requirements of whoever happens to be governing, so that history reaches the man the way it reaches most people: as a change in what the troupe is permitted to perform. Occupation is not staged as an event with a date. It is a set of conditions that alters the repertoire. Li Tien-lu recalls all of it himself, which puts a voice in the film older than its images. TSPDT's thousand greatest, the Golden Horse hundred, a jury prize for direction: the record on this one is not in dispute.

A great many listeners met bossa nova here first, in a score by Luiz Bonfá and Antonio Carlos Jobim. The film moves the legend of Orpheus and Eurydice to the hills above Rio during Carnaval and does not treat the transposition as a stunt: two lovers crossing a city that is dancing, a fiancée with a grievance, a man in costume who means them harm, a myth obliged to survive contact with an actual crowd. Marcel Camus keeps fantasy and plain fact on the same footing across a hundred minutes that rarely stand still. The Palme d'Or went to it, and the Academy's award for a film made outside the United States. What travelled furthest, though, was the sound: the picture carried a new Brazilian music out and the music kept going.

A farce about a timid schoolteacher asking his repellent friend for lessons in seduction is not the usual shape of a Palme d'Or winner. Eighty-five minutes, London, 1965, and Richard Lester shoots the city as though it were being repossessed by everyone under thirty: rooms emptied out, a stranger painting every surface white, dialogue arriving faster than the frame can hold it. The premise is period-typical and the film understands it better than its characters do, since the friend's method is presented as method, which is to say as something learned, boastful and thin. Then a woman new to town declines to behave as either man has arranged for. The joke lands on the instruction rather than on the pupil, and that is why it still runs.

A wealthy man's daughter wants her father's servant, and the servant is bitter, competent, and entirely aware of what the wanting is worth. Strindberg wrote the play; Alf Sjöberg had to decide how much of the theatre to keep, and the ninety minutes that result put the house, the kitchen and the grounds to work on arguments that dialogue alone would otherwise carry. What is at stake is position, not romance. Julie can treat it as an episode. Jean has been calculating for years, and calculation is the only shape desire can take between two people forbidden to address each other as equals. Sweden, 1951: a Palme d'Or and a directing prize for a chamber piece that keeps class and sex in the same room and will not separate them.

Nearly three hours, and the whole span sits before the shooting starts, 1939 to the first of November, 1954. Mohammed Lakhdar-Hamina is making an argument rather than a battle picture: that the war in Algeria was no accident of history but the surfacing of something accumulating since 1830, through suffering and through revolts that did not hold. Ahmed arrives at political consciousness slowly, his son watching him do it, while Miloud, half prophet and half nuisance, carries the popular memory of everything already attempted. The length is part of the case, a country telling its own long story at its own chosen pace, in Arabic, in 1975, within living memory of the events. It holds a Palme d'Or and a prize for direction.

Two soldiers from opposing armies end up in the same trench, and neither one can leave it. What follows is all negotiation: between two men who share a language and nothing else, between armies that accept a ceasefire because refusing would look bad, and inside a UN command where a request for help becomes a question of whose office it belongs to. Danis Tanović wrote the film as well as directing it, and the writing is where it lives, ninety-eight minutes in which procedure turns out to be funnier and more frightening than combat. Bosnian dialogue, French financing, 2001, close enough to the war that the jokes still have edges on them. The Academy's international award went to it, with European prizes for the screenplay and the lead.

A stolen car turns out to have a baby in the back seat, and the thief becomes something else before he has decided anything. Gavin Hood sets this outside Johannesburg and keeps it in Tswana, ninety-four minutes at the pace of a boy who left home young and has since made a name for himself out of the word for gangster. The machinery is old, a hard young man and an infant and a conscience arriving late, and the film does not pretend to have invented it. What it has instead is address. It looks at what a stolen car is worth, at what an infant costs in attention and time to keep alive, and at how recently the thief was a child himself, and it declines to make any of it picturesque. The Academy's international award went to it; so did an audience prize.

A small farm passes from a late mother to her daughter in a Dutch village just after the war, and the inheritance turns out to be a foundation. Marleen Gorris moves four generations through 102 minutes, Antonia and Danielle and the two who come after them, which means the film advances in seasons and decades rather than in scenes. The village supplies what villages supply: a suitor who will not be discouraged, a recluse called Crooked Finger, opinion. The comedy is dry; the anger underneath it is not. TakeScore puts the durable value at 68 out of 100. Gorris is interested in what a household looks like once it is run entirely by women out of the habit of asking permission, and the oddity is that she presents this as ordinary rather than as a case being made.
